title: What is React?
description: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of small, reusable pieces called components.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content:
React is an open-source JavaScript library, created at Meta, for building user interfaces. You describe **what** the UI should look like for a given state, and React works out **how** to update the screen.

React itself focuses on the view layer. Routing, data fetching and bundling come from frameworks such as Next.js or React Router, or from tools such as Vite.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Manually updating the DOM (`document.querySelector(...).textContent = ...`) gets error-prone as apps grow: you must remember every place that depends on a piece of data. React lets you write the UI as a function of state. When state changes, React re-runs your components and updates only what changed.

sections.title: How does it work?
sections.content:
- You write components: functions that return JSX.
- React calls them to produce a description of the UI.
- When state changes, React calls them again, compares the new description with the previous one, and commits the minimal DOM changes.

codeExamples.title: Your first component
codeExamples.explanation: `Greeting` is a component: a plain function that receives props and returns JSX. `App` renders it with `name="Ada"`. You never touch the DOM directly — React does that for you.

commonMistakes: Calling React a full framework. React is a UI library; frameworks like Next.js add routing, data fetching and rendering strategies.
Thinking React re-renders the whole page on every change. It re-runs components, but only commits the DOM changes that are actually needed.
realWorldExample: Facebook, Instagram, Netflix, Airbnb and the Next.js ecosystem all build interfaces with React components.
interviewTip: Say "React is a declarative, component-based library for building UIs" and give the formula UI = f(state). Mention that frameworks such as Next.js build on top of it.

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes React?
options: A full-stack framework with a built-in database
A JavaScript library for building user interfaces with components
quiz.explanation: React is a UI library. Frameworks like Next.js add routing, data fetching and server rendering on top of it.

quiz.prompt: In React you normally update the DOM yourself with `document.querySelector`.
quiz.explanation: You update state; React updates the DOM.

flashcards.back: UI is a function of state: same state, same UI.
Meta and the open-source community.

interviewQuestion.question: What does "declarative" mean in React?
interviewQuestion.answer: You describe the desired UI for the current state, and React figures out the DOM operations. In an imperative approach you write each DOM mutation step by step yourself.

title: Why React?
description: The problems React solves and the trade-offs it brings.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: "Why React?" is about the benefits that made React the most widely used UI library: reusable components, one-way data flow, a declarative model and an enormous ecosystem.

sections.title: Why does it matter?
sections.content:
- **Composition:** build complex screens from small, testable components.
- **Predictability:** data flows down through props, so it is easier to trace where values come from.
- **Ecosystem:** Next.js, React Native, testing tools, component libraries and a large hiring market.
- **Modern capabilities:** Server Components, Actions, Suspense and streaming let React span server and client.

sections.title: When is React a good fit?
sections.content: Interactive apps with lots of changing state: dashboards, editors, e-commerce, social feeds and design systems shared across teams.

codeExamples.title: Reuse in practice
codeExamples.explanation: One `Button` component captures styling and behaviour. Every screen reuses it, so a design change happens in one place.

whenNotToUse: A simple static page with little interactivity.
Content that must be readable without JavaScript, unless you render it on the server (e.g. with Next.js).
commonMistakes: Choosing React for a mostly static content site where plain HTML or a static site generator would be simpler.
Assuming React alone handles routing, SEO and data fetching — those usually come from a framework.
realWorldExample: Design systems such as Material UI or Shopify Polaris ship as React component libraries reused across hundreds of screens.
interviewTip: Balance pros with trade-offs (bundle size, needing a framework for SEO/SSR). Interviewers like candidates who know when NOT to use a tool.

quiz.prompt: Which is a core benefit of React's one-way data flow?
options: It removes the need for state
Data can be changed from any component freely
It's easier to trace where data comes from and how it changes
quiz.explanation: Props flow from parent to child, which makes data easier to follow and debug.

flashcards.back: JavaScript bundle size and needing extra tools for routing, SSR and SEO.

title: Starting a React Project in 2026
description: How to start a new React app today — with a framework or with Vite.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content:
The React team recommends starting new apps with a **framework** such as Next.js or React Router (framework mode). If you need a client-only app, a build tool such as **Vite** is the common choice.

Create React App (CRA) was officially deprecated in February 2025 and should not be used for new projects.

sections.title: Why does it matter?
sections.content: Frameworks solve problems every real app hits: routing, data fetching, code splitting, server rendering and deployment. Starting with one avoids re-inventing these later.

sections.title: How do you do it?
sections.content:
- Full-stack / SEO-sensitive app: `npx create-next-app@latest`
- Client-only SPA: `npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts`
- Run `npm run dev` and open the local URL.

codeExamples.title: Creating projects
codeExamples.code:
# Full-stack React with the App Router
npx create-next-app@latest my-app

# Client-side React with Vite + TypeScript
npm create vite@latest my-spa -- --template react-ts
cd my-spa
npm install
npm run dev
codeExamples.explanation: `create-next-app` scaffolds a Next.js project (TypeScript, ESLint and Tailwind are offered during setup). The Vite template gives a fast dev server with hot module replacement.

commonMistakes: Following old tutorials that use `create-react-app`.
Picking a client-only SPA for a content site that needs SEO.
realWorldExample: Most new production React apps at startups today begin with `create-next-app` or a Vite template.
interviewTip: If asked how you'd start a project, mention the framework recommendation, why CRA is deprecated, and when a Vite SPA is still fine.

quiz.prompt: Create React App is the recommended way to start new React projects in 2026.
quiz.explanation: CRA was deprecated in 2025. Use a framework like Next.js, or Vite for client-only apps.

flashcards.front: Recommended way to start a full-stack React app?
flashcards.back: Use a framework, e.g. `npx create-next-app@latest`.

title: Components
description: Components are reusable functions that return UI. They are the building blocks of every React app.

sections.title: What are components?
sections.content: A component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX. Its name must start with a capital letter so React can tell `<Profile />` (your component) from `<div>` (an HTML tag).

sections.title: Why do they exist?
sections.content: Components let you split the UI into independent, reusable pieces and think about each one in isolation. A page is just components nested inside components.

sections.title: How do they work?
sections.content: React calls your component function during rendering. It reads its props, returns JSX, and React turns that JSX into DOM nodes. Modern React uses **function components**; class components still work but are legacy for new code.

codeExamples.title: Composing components
codeExamples.explanation: `UserCard` composes `Avatar`. Each component has one job, and both can be reused independently.

commonMistakes: Naming components in lowercase (`function card()`): React treats `<card>` as an HTML tag.
Defining a component inside another component — it is re-created on every render and loses its state.
Making components too big; extract pieces when a component handles several concerns.
realWorldExample: An e-commerce product page is made of `ProductGallery`, `PriceTag`, `AddToCartButton` and `ReviewList` components.
interviewTip: Know why components must be capitalised, and why you should never declare a component inside another component's body.

quiz.prompt: Why must component names start with a capital letter?
options: Capitalised names are required by JavaScript
So JSX can distinguish components from built-in HTML tags
quiz.explanation: Lowercase JSX tags are treated as HTML elements, so `<card />` would create an unknown `card` element.

quiz.prompt: Defining a component inside another component's body is safe and recommended.
quiz.explanation: It creates a new component type every render and resets its state.

flashcards.back: JSX describing part of the UI (or null).

flashcards.front: Modern default: function or class components?
flashcards.back: Function components with Hooks.

beforeAfter.title: Never define components inside components
beforeAfter.explanation: A component declared inside another is a brand-new function each render, so React sees a different component type and remounts it, wiping its state. Declare components at module level.

title: Component Composition & children
description: Build flexible components by nesting them and passing UI through `children`.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Composition means building components by combining other components. The special `children` prop holds whatever you place between a component's opening and closing tags.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: React favours composition over inheritance. Instead of subclassing, you create generic wrappers (`Card`, `Modal`, `Layout`) and pass content in. This also helps avoid prop drilling — you can pass already-rendered elements down.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content:
- Layout and container components (cards, dialogs, pages).
- "Slots": pass multiple pieces of UI as named props like `header` and `footer`.
- Avoiding deep prop drilling by composing at the top level.

codeExamples.title: children and named slots
codeExamples.explanation:
`children` receives the `

` element; `actions` is a named slot receiving a button. `Card` doesn't need to know what it wraps.

commonMistakes: Passing many configuration props when passing JSX as `children` would be simpler.
Reaching for Context to avoid prop drilling when composition would solve it.
realWorldExample: Dialog libraries expose `<Dialog><Dialog.Title/>...</Dialog>` APIs built entirely on composition.
interviewTip: Explain that composition can solve prop drilling: render the deep child at the top and pass it down as `children`.

quiz.prompt: What is the `children` prop?
options: A list of child components' state
A reference to the DOM node
Whatever JSX is placed between a component's opening and closing tags
quiz.explanation: `children` is the content nested inside the component tags.

flashcards.back: React recommends composition; inheritance between components is almost never needed.

title: Keeping Components Pure
description: Rendering must be a pure calculation: same inputs, same output, no side effects.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: A pure component returns the same JSX for the same props, state and context, and does not change anything that existed before it was called.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: React may call your components more than once, in any order, or pause and resume rendering (concurrent features). That's only safe if rendering has no side effects. Purity also enables caching (memo, React Compiler) and Server Components.

sections.title: How to keep components pure
sections.content:
- Don't mutate props, state or variables declared outside the component.
- Put side effects (fetching, subscriptions, timers, logging) in event handlers or `useEffect`.
- Creating and mutating *local* variables inside render is fine.

codeExamples.title: Impure vs pure
codeExamples.explanation: `BadCup` shows different numbers each time React renders it — and Strict Mode's double render in development makes the bug obvious. `Cup` always renders the same output for the same `guest` prop.

commonMistakes: Mutating props or state objects directly (`props.items.push(x)`).
Calling APIs, setting timers or writing to localStorage during render.
realWorldExample: The React Compiler and `React.memo` rely on purity to skip work safely.
interviewTip: Connect purity to Strict Mode: React double-invokes render in development to surface impure components.

quiz.prompt: Creating and mutating a local array inside a component's render is fine.
quiz.explanation: Local mutation is fine — it doesn't affect anything outside the render.

quiz.prompt: Where should side effects like data subscriptions go?
quiz.explanation: Render must be pure; effects belong in event handlers or Effects.

flashcards.front: Why does Strict Mode render twice in dev?
flashcards.back: To help find impure rendering logic.

title: JSX
description: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript.

sections.title: What is JSX?
sections.content: JSX looks like HTML but lives in JavaScript. A compiler (Babel, SWC, esbuild) turns it into function calls that create React elements.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Rendering logic and markup are tightly coupled, so React keeps them together in components. JSX makes that markup readable while still being plain JavaScript under the hood.

sections.title: Rules of JSX
sections.content:
- Return a single root element; use a Fragment `<>...` to group without extra DOM. - Close all tags: ``, `
`. - Use camelCase attributes: `className`, `htmlFor`, `onClick`, `tabIndex`. - Put JavaScript **expressions** inside `{}` — not statements like `if` or `for`.

codeExamples.title: JSX with expressions
codeExamples.explanation: Curly braces embed JavaScript expressions. The style prop takes an object, hence the double braces. The Fragment groups both elements without adding a wrapper `div`.

commonMistakes: Using `class` instead of `className`.
Trying to use `if` statements inside `{}` — use a ternary, `&&`, or compute values before `return`.
Forgetting that JSX must return one root element.
realWorldExample: Every React codebase uses JSX (or TSX in TypeScript projects).
interviewTip: Mention that JSX is optional syntax that compiles to `jsx()` calls from `react/jsx-runtime` (the modern automatic runtime), so you no longer need `import React` just for JSX.

quiz.prompt: Which attribute sets a CSS class in JSX?
quiz.explanation: `class` is a reserved word in JavaScript, so JSX uses `className`.

quiz.prompt: What renders?
quiz.explanation: `0 && ...` evaluates to `0`, and React renders numbers. Use `items > 0 && ...` instead.

flashcards.front: How do you return two siblings without a wrapper div?
flashcards.back: Wrap them in a Fragment: `<>...</>`.
Any JavaScript expression (not statements).

interviewQuestion.question: Is JSX required to use React? What does it compile to?
interviewQuestion.answer: No. JSX is syntactic sugar. With the modern automatic runtime it compiles to calls like `jsx('h1', { children: 'Hi' })` imported from `react/jsx-runtime`. Older setups compiled to `React.createElement`.

title: Conditional Rendering
description: Show different UI depending on conditions using plain JavaScript.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Conditional rendering means choosing what to render based on state or props. React has no special syntax — you use JavaScript: `if`, ternaries and `&&`.

sections.title: How to do it
sections.content:
- **Early return** for whole-component branches: `if (!user) return <Login />;`
- **Ternary** for either/or: `{isOpen ? <Panel /> : <Teaser />}`
- **&&** for show/hide: `{error && <ErrorBanner />}`
- Return `null` to render nothing.

sections.title: When to extract
sections.content: When conditions nest more than one level, move the logic into a variable or a small component to keep JSX readable.

codeExamples.title: All three patterns
codeExamples.explanation: The early return handles the signed-out case. The ternary switches between spinner and list. `messages.length > 0 &&` avoids accidentally rendering `0`.

commonMistakes: Rendering `0` with `{count && <Badge />}` — use `count > 0 &&`.
Deeply nested ternaries that are hard to read.
realWorldExample: Dashboards render skeleton loaders, empty states and error banners conditionally.
interviewTip: Point out the `0 &&` pitfall — interviewers love it.

quiz.prompt: What is rendered when `count` is 0?
quiz.explanation: `0` is falsy but still a renderable number, so React prints 0.

flashcards.front: How do you render nothing from a component?
flashcards.back: Return `null`.

title: Rendering Lists
description: Turn arrays of data into arrays of elements with `map()`.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: To render a list you transform data into JSX with `array.map()`. Each item needs a `key` so React can track it between renders.

sections.title: How does it work?
sections.content: `map` returns an array of elements, and React renders arrays directly. Filter or sort the data **before** mapping, and extract complex items into their own component.

codeExamples.title: Filter and map
codeExamples.explanation: `filter` removes out-of-stock items, then `map` turns each product into an `<li>` with a stable `key` taken from its id.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the `key` prop.
Sorting with `products.sort()` in render — it mutates the prop. Use `[...products].sort()` or `toSorted()`.
realWorldExample: Search results, chat messages and table rows are all rendered with `map`.
interviewTip: Mention that `toSorted()`, `toReversed()` and spread copies avoid mutating props during render.

quiz.prompt: `items.sort()` inside render is safe because it returns a new array.
quiz.explanation: `sort()` mutates the original array. Use `toSorted()` or copy first.

flashcards.front: Which array method renders a list?
flashcards.back: `map()`, returning JSX for each item.

title: Keys
description: Keys tell React which list item is which, so it can preserve state and update efficiently.
keyConcepts: Avoid index keys for dynamic lists

sections.title: What are keys?
sections.content: A `key` is a special prop that gives each element in a list a stable identity among its siblings. React uses it during reconciliation to match old and new items.

sections.title: Why are they important?
sections.content: Without stable keys, React matches items by position. When you insert, delete or reorder items, state (like input text or focus) can end up attached to the wrong item, and React does more DOM work than needed.

sections.title: Good and bad keys
sections.content:
- Good: database ids, UUIDs created when the item is created, unique slugs.
- Risky: array index — fine only for static lists that never reorder.
- Wrong: `Math.random()` — a new key each render remounts every item.

sections.title: Keys outside lists
sections.content: Changing a component's `key` forces React to remount it with fresh state — a handy way to reset a form when switching between users: `<Profile key={userId} />`.

codeExamples.title: Resetting state with a key
codeExamples.explanation: When `contact.id` changes, React sees a different key, unmounts the old `MessageDraft` and mounts a new one, so the draft text never leaks between conversations.

commonMistakes: Using the array index as key for lists that can reorder or have items removed.
Generating keys with `Math.random()` or `crypto.randomUUID()` during render.
realWorldExample: In a todo list using index keys, deleting the first item makes the second item's checkbox state appear on the wrong row.
interviewTip: Explain keys in terms of reconciliation: they let React match elements across renders. Then mention the reset-state trick.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best key for a list of users fetched from an API?
quiz.explanation: A stable, unique id from the data is ideal.

quiz.prompt: Changing a component's key causes React to remount it with fresh state.
quiz.explanation: A new key means a new component identity.

flashcards.back: Among siblings in the same list — not globally.

flashcards.front: Trick to reset a component's state?
flashcards.back: Change its `key`.

beforeAfter.title: Index keys vs stable ids
beforeAfter.explanation: With index keys, removing an item shifts every following key, so each `TodoItem` receives a different todo but keeps its old internal state. Stable ids keep identity attached to the data.

title: Props
description: Props are the inputs a parent passes to a child component. They are read-only.

sections.title: What are props?
sections.content: Props (properties) are the arguments of a component. A parent passes them like HTML attributes, and the child receives them as one object.

sections.title: Why do they exist?
sections.content: Props make components configurable and reusable. They also define one-way data flow: data moves from parents to children, which makes apps predictable.

sections.title: Rules
sections.content:
- Props are **read-only**. Never modify them; ask the parent to change its state instead (by calling a function prop).
- Use destructuring with defaults: `function Button({ size = 'md' })`.
- Any value can be a prop: strings, numbers, objects, functions, JSX.

codeExamples.title: Data down, events up
codeExamples.explanation: The parent owns the state and passes `value` down. The child reports clicks up through the `onIncrement` function prop.

commonMistakes: Mutating props (`props.user.name = 'x'`).
Copying props into state without a reason, which creates two sources of truth.
realWorldExample: A `Button` component receives `variant`, `disabled` and `onClick` props from every screen that uses it.
interviewTip: Describe props as function arguments and stress they are immutable from the child's perspective.

quiz.prompt: A child component may modify the props it receives.
quiz.explanation: Props are read-only. Children request changes via callback props.

quiz.prompt: How does a child tell its parent something happened?
options: By calling a function passed as a prop
By reading the parent's state directly
quiz.explanation: Function props like `onChange` let children send events up.

flashcards.back: One-way: from parent to child via props.

title: State
description: State is a component's memory: data that changes over time and triggers re-renders.

sections.title: What is state?
sections.content: State is data a component remembers between renders, such as form input, whether a menu is open, or the current page. Updating it with its setter tells React to re-render.

sections.title: Props vs state
sections.content: Props are passed in by the parent and are read-only. State is owned and updated by the component itself. A parent's state often becomes a child's props.

sections.title: How updates work
sections.content:
- State is a **snapshot**: inside one render, `count` never changes, even after calling `setCount`.
- React **batches** multiple updates in the same event into one re-render.
- Treat objects and arrays as immutable: create new copies instead of mutating.

codeExamples.title: Immutable updates
codeExamples.explanation: `setUser` receives a function of the previous state and returns a **new** object with a **new** tags array. Mutating `user.tags.push()` would not trigger a re-render because the reference wouldn't change.

commonMistakes: Mutating state objects or arrays directly.
Expecting the state variable to update immediately after calling the setter.
Storing values in state that can be computed from props or other state.
realWorldExample: A shopping cart keeps its items in state; adding an item creates a new array so React re-renders the cart badge.
interviewTip: Use the phrase "state is a snapshot" and explain why `setCount(count + 1)` three times only adds one.

quiz.prompt: What does the button show after one click?
quiz.explanation: Each call uses the same snapshot (`count` is 0), so all three set it to 1. Use `setCount(c => c + 1)` to add 3.

quiz.prompt: Calling `user.tags.push('x')` and then `setUser(user)` reliably re-renders.
quiz.explanation: The object reference is unchanged, so React may bail out. Create a new object.

flashcards.front: Props vs state in one line?
flashcards.back: Props come from the parent and are read-only; state is owned by the component and changes over time.

flashcards.front: Why use the updater form setX(prev => ...)?
flashcards.back: To compute from the latest state, e.g. multiple updates in one event.

title: Lifting State Up
description: Move shared state to the closest common parent so sibling components stay in sync.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: When two components need the same data, you remove the state from both and keep it in their closest common parent. The parent passes the value and an updater function down as props.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Duplicated state drifts out of sync. Lifting state creates a single source of truth, so every component shows consistent data.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content:
- Accordions where only one panel may be open.
- Filters that affect a sibling list.
- Form inputs whose values a sibling preview displays.

codeExamples.title: Accordion with lifted state
codeExamples.explanation: The parent owns `activeIndex`, so opening one panel automatically closes the other. Each `Panel` is now controlled by props.

commonMistakes: Lifting state too high (e.g. to the app root), causing unnecessary re-renders.
Keeping a copy of the lifted value in child state.
realWorldExample: A product filter sidebar and the results grid share filter state lifted to the page component.
interviewTip: Say "single source of truth" and mention lifting only as high as needed; when it gets deep consider composition or context.

quiz.prompt: Two sibling components need the same data. What's the usual React solution?
options: Lift state to their closest common parent
quiz.explanation: Lifting state to the common parent creates a single source of truth.

flashcards.back: In the closest common parent of the components that need it.

title: Derived State
description: Don't store what you can calculate. Compute values during render instead.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Derived state is any value that can be computed from existing props or state — for example a filtered list, a total price or a full name.

sections.title: Why avoid storing it?
sections.content: Storing derived values in state means keeping two things in sync. That usually requires an extra `useEffect` that causes an extra render and opens the door to bugs where the copies disagree.

sections.title: How to do it
sections.content: Calculate during render. If the calculation is genuinely expensive and you have measured it, wrap it in `useMemo` (or let the React Compiler memoize it).

codeExamples.title: Calculating instead of syncing
codeExamples.explanation: `subtotal`, `discount` and `total` are derived on every render. There's no state or Effect to keep them in sync — they can't be wrong.

whenNotToUse: Don't use derived values when you need to remember user edits independently of the source (that's real state).
commonMistakes: Using `useEffect` + `setState` to compute a filtered list.
Initialising state from a prop and expecting it to update when the prop changes.
realWorldExample: A table's "selected count" should be `selectedIds.length`, not a separate counter in state.
interviewTip: Interviewers often ask "you might not need an Effect" questions. Show the before/after of removing an Effect that syncs derived state.

quiz.prompt: You should store `fullName` in state when you already have `firstName` and `lastName` in state.
quiz.explanation: Compute `firstName + ' ' + lastName` during render instead.

flashcards.front: Rule of thumb for derived values?
flashcards.back: If it can be computed from props/state, compute it during render.

beforeAfter.title: Remove the syncing Effect
beforeAfter.after:
const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);
const visible = todos.filter(t => !t.done);
beforeAfter.explanation: The Effect version renders twice (once stale, once updated) and adds state that can drift. Computing during render is simpler and always correct.

title: State Synchronization & Single Source of Truth
description: Avoid keeping copies of the same data in multiple places, and know when syncing is genuinely needed.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: State synchronization is keeping two pieces of data consistent. In React, the best synchronization is usually none: keep one source of truth and derive or pass everything else.

sections.title: Common cases
sections.content:
- **Prop copied to state:** only valid as an *initial* value (name it `initialColor`).
- **Reset when an id changes:** use a `key` instead of an Effect.
- **Sync with an external system** (a chart library, a WebSocket, the URL): that's what `useEffect` is for.

sections.title: Store ids, not copies
sections.content: When selecting an item from a list, store `selectedId` rather than a copy of the selected object. Then derive it: `items.find(i => i.id === selectedId)`. Edits to the list are reflected automatically.

codeExamples.title: Store the id, derive the object
codeExamples.explanation: If a message is edited or deleted, `selected` updates automatically. Storing a copy of the message object would show stale data.

commonMistakes: `useState(props.value)` and expecting it to follow later prop changes.
Using an Effect to reset state when a prop changes instead of a `key`.
realWorldExample: Master-detail screens (email clients, admin panels) store the selected id and derive the detail.
interviewTip: Mention the React docs guidance "You Might Not Need an Effect" and give the `selectedId` example.

quiz.prompt: A child copies a prop into state with useState(props.color). What happens when the parent later changes color?
options: The state keeps the initial value
quiz.explanation: The useState initial value is only used on the first render.

flashcards.front: Store selected item or selected id?
flashcards.back: Store the id; derive the item from the list.

title: Handling Events
description: Respond to clicks, typing and other user actions with event handler props.
keyConcepts: Pass a function, don't call it

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Event handlers are functions you pass to JSX props such as `onClick`, `onChange` or `onSubmit`. React calls them when the event happens.

sections.title: How does it work?
sections.content: React wraps native events in a cross-browser **SyntheticEvent** with the same interface (`e.target`, `e.preventDefault()`, `e.stopPropagation()`). React attaches listeners at the root container and dispatches them to your handlers.

sections.title: Rules
sections.content:
- Pass the function: `onClick={handleClick}` — not `onClick={handleClick()}`.
- To pass arguments, wrap it: `onClick={() => remove(item.id)}`.
- Event handlers are the right place for side effects (API calls, navigation).

codeExamples.title: Handlers with arguments
codeExamples.explanation: Clicking the row toggles the todo. The delete button stops propagation so the click doesn't bubble up to the `li` and toggle it as well.

commonMistakes: Writing `onClick={doSomething()}`, which calls the function during render.
Forgetting `e.preventDefault()` on form submits in client-only forms.
realWorldExample: Every button, menu, drag-and-drop interaction and keyboard shortcut is wired through event handlers.
interviewTip: Explain the difference between passing a function and calling it, and mention SyntheticEvent.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct?
quiz.explanation: Pass the function reference; React calls it on click.

flashcards.back: It calls `handle` during render instead of on click.

title: Forms in Modern React
description: Build forms with controlled inputs or with React 19 form Actions.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Forms collect user input. In React you can manage each field in state (controlled), read values on submit with `FormData`, or — since React 19 — pass a function to `<form action={...}>`.

sections.title: Why does it matter?
sections.content: Forms are where most user data enters an app. Good forms validate input, show pending states, handle errors and are accessible.

sections.title: Options
sections.content:
- **Controlled inputs:** best for instant validation and dependent fields.
- **FormData on submit:** less code for simple forms.
- **React 19 Actions:** `<form action={submit}>` passes a `FormData` to your function, handles pending state with `useFormStatus`/`useActionState`, and resets uncontrolled fields after success.

codeExamples.title: A form Action (React 19)
codeExamples.explanation: React calls `subscribe` with the form's `FormData`. `useFormStatus` (from `react-dom`) reads the pending state of the parent form, so the button can disable itself while the Action runs.

commonMistakes: Inputs without a `<label>`, which hurts accessibility.
Calling `useFormStatus` in the same component that renders the `<form>` — it must be in a child.
Missing `name` attributes, so values don't appear in FormData.
realWorldExample: Sign-up, checkout and comment forms combine validation, pending states and error messages.
interviewTip: Mention both styles and React 19's form Actions with `useActionState` and `useFormStatus`.

quiz.prompt: `useFormStatus` must be called from a component rendered inside the `<form>`.
quiz.explanation: It reads the status of the parent form, so it can't be in the component that renders the form itself.

quiz.prompt: In React 19, what does a function passed to `<form action={fn}>` receive?
quiz.explanation: Form Actions receive the submitted FormData.

flashcards.back: `react-dom`.

flashcards.front: What attribute puts a field into FormData?
flashcards.back: `name`.

title: Controlled Components
description: An input whose value is driven by React state.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: A controlled input gets its `value` from state and reports changes through `onChange`. React state is the single source of truth for what the field shows.

sections.title: Why use it?
sections.content: Because you hold the value at all times you can validate on every keystroke, format input (e.g. uppercase, masks), disable buttons and keep several fields in sync.

sections.title: How it works
sections.content: Every keystroke calls `onChange`, you update state, React re-renders and the input shows the new value. If you set `value` without `onChange`, the input becomes read-only.

codeExamples.title: Validated controlled input
codeExamples.explanation: The input always shows `username` from state. The handler lowercases text as the user types, and validation is derived during render.

commonMistakes: Setting `value` without `onChange` (read-only input warning).
Switching an input from uncontrolled to controlled by starting with `undefined` — initialise with `''`.
realWorldExample: Search boxes that filter as you type and credit-card fields with formatting are controlled inputs.
interviewTip: Contrast with uncontrolled components and mention the 'changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled' warning.

quiz.prompt: What makes an input 'controlled'?
options: Its value comes from React state with an onChange handler
quiz.explanation: `value` + `onChange` driven by state.

flashcards.front: Initial value for a controlled text input?
flashcards.back: An empty string `''`, never undefined.

title: Uncontrolled Components
description: Let the DOM hold the input's value and read it when needed.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: An uncontrolled input keeps its own value in the DOM. You give it an initial `defaultValue` and read the current value later — through a ref or from `FormData` on submit.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content:
- Simple forms where you only need values on submit.
- `<input type="file">`, which is always uncontrolled.
- Integrating with non-React code.
- React 19 form Actions work naturally with uncontrolled inputs.

codeExamples.title: Reading values on submit
codeExamples.explanation: The textarea manages its own value. On submit, `FormData` reads every named field. No state updates happen while typing.

commonMistakes: Using `value` instead of `defaultValue` for an uncontrolled field.
Trying to make a file input controlled.
realWorldExample: Large settings forms often read values once on submit rather than re-rendering on every keystroke.
interviewTip: Explain the trade-off: fewer re-renders and less code vs. less control over live validation.

quiz.prompt: `<input type="file">` can be a controlled component.
quiz.explanation: Its value is read-only for security reasons, so it's always uncontrolled.

flashcards.back: `defaultValue` (or `defaultChecked`).

title: useState
description: The Hook that adds state to function components.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useState(initialValue)` returns a pair: the current value and a setter. Calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value.

sections.title: Syntax
sections.content:
`const [count, setCount] = useState(0);`

- `setCount(5)` replaces the value.
- `setCount(c => c + 1)` computes from the previous value.
- `useState(() => expensiveInit())` runs the initializer only on the first render.

sections.title: How does it work?
sections.content: React stores state per component instance, in call order. That's why Hooks must be called in the same order on every render. If you set the same value (by `Object.is`), React may skip re-rendering.

codeExamples.title: Updater and lazy initialiser
codeExamples.explanation: Passing a function to `useState` avoids re-reading storage on every render. The updater form `prev => ...` always works on the latest state, even with several updates queued.

commonMistakes: `useState(expensive())` — runs `expensive` every render; pass `() => expensive()` instead.
Reading state right after setting it and expecting the new value.
realWorldExample: Toggles, form fields, selected tabs and open/closed dialogs all use `useState`.
interviewTip: Know the updater form, lazy initialisation and that updates are batched.

quiz.prompt: When does the initializer in `useState(() => compute())` run?
quiz.explanation: Lazy initializers run once, during the initial render.

quiz.prompt: Calling setCount with the same value always forces a re-render.
quiz.explanation: React compares with Object.is and may bail out.

title: useEffect
description: Synchronize a component with an external system after React commits to the screen.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useEffect(setup, dependencies)` runs `setup` after the component renders and the DOM is updated. It's for synchronizing with things **outside** React: network subscriptions, timers, browser APIs, third-party widgets.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Rendering must be pure, but apps still need side effects. Effects give you a place to run them after commit, and a cleanup function to undo them.

sections.title: Dependencies
sections.content:
- No array: runs after every render.
- `[]`: runs after the first mount (and cleanup on unmount).
- `[a, b]`: re-runs when `a` or `b` change (compared with `Object.is`).

List every reactive value the effect reads. The `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` rules catch missing ones.

sections.title: Why does it run twice in development?
sections.content: In Strict Mode, React mounts, unmounts and re-mounts components once in development. Your effect runs setup → cleanup → setup. This surfaces missing cleanup. It does not happen in production.

codeExamples.title: Subscription with cleanup
codeExamples.explanation: When `roomId` changes, React runs the cleanup (disconnects from the old room) and then the setup for the new room. On unmount, it disconnects.

whenNotToUse: Transforming data for rendering — compute it during render.
Handling user actions — use event handlers.
Fetching in frameworks that offer server data fetching (e.g. Server Components in Next.js).
commonMistakes: Using an Effect to compute derived data or to handle a user event.
Lying about dependencies to stop re-runs, causing stale values.
Fetching without handling race conditions (use an `ignore` flag or AbortController).
realWorldExample: Connecting to a WebSocket, syncing with a map widget, or adding a `resize` listener are classic Effects.
interviewTip: Say: Effects are for synchronizing with external systems, not for data flow. Explain the dev-only double run in Strict Mode.

quiz.prompt: Order what happens when `roomId` changes:
items: Component re-renders with the new roomId
Cleanup runs for the old roomId
Setup runs for the new roomId
quiz.explanation: React renders, commits, then runs the previous effect's cleanup before the new setup.

quiz.prompt: An effect with an empty dependency array `[]` runs…
options: After the initial mount only (plus cleanup on unmount)
quiz.explanation: In production, once after mount. In development Strict Mode, it runs setup → cleanup → setup.

flashcards.back: Synchronizing with an external system.
Before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts.

interviewQuestion.question: Why does useEffect run twice in development?
interviewQuestion.answer: React Strict Mode intentionally mounts, unmounts and remounts components in development to check that effects clean up properly. If your effect breaks when it runs twice, it's missing cleanup. Production runs it once.

title: useRef
description: Keep a mutable value that survives re-renders without causing them, or reference a DOM node.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useRef(initial)` returns an object `{ current: initial }` that stays the same across renders. Changing `ref.current` does **not** trigger a re-render.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content:
- Access DOM nodes: focus an input, measure size, scroll into view.
- Store values that aren't needed for rendering: timer ids, previous values, WebSocket instances.

sections.title: React 19 change
sections.content: Function components can now receive `ref` as a normal prop, so `forwardRef` is no longer needed for new code. Ref callbacks may also return a cleanup function.

codeExamples.title: Focusing an input
codeExamples.explanation: React sets `inputRef.current` to the DOM node after commit. Clicking the button calls the native `focus()`. In React 19, `TextInput` receives `ref` directly as a prop.

commonMistakes: Reading or writing `ref.current` during render (it makes rendering impure).
Using a ref for values that should update the UI — use state instead.
realWorldExample: Auto-focusing a modal's first field, storing an `IntersectionObserver`, or keeping a debounce timer id.
interviewTip: Compare useRef vs useState: both persist across renders; only state changes trigger re-renders.

quiz.prompt: Updating `ref.current` causes the component to re-render.
quiz.explanation: Refs are mutable boxes; changing them doesn't re-render.

quiz.prompt: In React 19, how does a function component accept a ref?
quiz.explanation: React 19 passes `ref` as a prop to function components.

flashcards.back: Both persist; only state triggers re-render.

title: useContext
description: Share values deep in the tree without passing props through every level.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Context lets a parent make a value available to every component below it. You create it with `createContext(default)`, provide it, and read it with `useContext(MyContext)` (or `use(MyContext)` in React 19).

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Passing the same prop through many layers (prop drilling) is tedious. Context is ideal for global-ish values: theme, current user, locale, feature flags.

sections.title: React 19 syntax
sections.content: You can render `<ThemeContext value="dark">` directly; `<ThemeContext.Provider>` still works but is the older form.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content: Every component that reads a context re-renders when its value changes. Keep values stable (memoize objects) and split unrelated data into separate contexts.

codeExamples.title: Theme context
codeExamples.explanation: `ThemedButton` reads the theme from the nearest provider above it, no matter how deep it is. When `theme` changes, readers re-render.

whenNotToUse: Values only one or two levels down — just pass props.
High-frequency updates consumed by many components — consider a dedicated store.
commonMistakes: Putting rapidly changing state in a single huge context that everything reads.
Passing a new object literal as the value on every render, re-rendering all consumers.
realWorldExample: Auth providers expose the current user; design systems expose theme tokens through context.
interviewTip: Mention that context is a transport mechanism, not a state manager, and discuss splitting contexts for performance.

quiz.prompt: What happens to components reading a context when its value changes?
quiz.explanation: All consumers re-render with the new value.

flashcards.back: Render `<MyContext value={...}>` directly.

title: Rules of Hooks
description: Two rules that make Hooks work: call them at the top level, and only from React functions.
keyConcepts: Only in components or custom hooks

sections.title: The rules
sections.content:
1. Only call Hooks **at the top level** — not inside conditions, loops, nested functions or after early returns.
2. Only call Hooks from **React function components** or **custom Hooks**.

(The `use()` API is the exception: it may be called conditionally.)

sections.title: Why do they exist?
sections.content: React identifies each Hook by its call order within a component. If a Hook is skipped on one render, every following Hook would read the wrong state.

sections.title: How to enforce them
sections.content: Use `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` (included in Next.js and Vite templates). It flags rule violations and missing Effect dependencies.

codeExamples.title: Conditional Hook fix
codeExamples.explanation: Moving the Hook above the early return guarantees the same Hook order on every render.

commonMistakes: Calling a Hook after an early `return`.
Calling Hooks inside event handlers or regular utility functions.
realWorldExample: Linting catches these at build time in every serious React codebase.
interviewTip: Explain *why* the rules exist (call order), not just what they are.

quiz.prompt: You can call useState inside an if statement if the condition rarely changes.
quiz.explanation: Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level.

flashcards.back: React matches Hooks to stored state by call order.

title: Custom Hooks
description: Extract reusable stateful logic into functions whose names start with `use`.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: A custom Hook is a function starting with `use` that calls other Hooks. It lets components share **logic** — each component that calls it gets its **own independent state**.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Before Hooks, sharing stateful logic required patterns like render props or higher-order components. Custom Hooks do the same with plain functions.

sections.title: Good custom Hooks
sections.content:
- Have a focused purpose: `useOnlineStatus`, `useDebouncedValue`, `useMediaQuery`.
- Hide implementation details behind a simple API.
- Avoid generic "lifecycle" Hooks like `useMount` that hide what the effect synchronizes with.

codeExamples.title: useDebouncedValue
codeExamples.explanation: The Hook owns a timer and its cleanup. Every component that uses it gets its own `debounced` state. `Search` stays focused on UI.

commonMistakes: Naming a function `useSomething` that doesn't call any Hooks.
Expecting two components using the same custom Hook to share state — they don't.
realWorldExample: Teams build libraries of Hooks such as `useAuth`, `useFeatureFlag`, `useLocalStorage`.
interviewTip: Stress: custom Hooks share logic, not state. Shared state needs lifting, context or a store.

quiz.prompt: Two components call `useCounter()`. Do they share the count?
options: No, each gets its own state
quiz.explanation: Each call creates independent state.

flashcards.back: Start with `use` so the Rules of Hooks can be enforced.

title: useReducer
description: Manage complex state transitions with a reducer function and dispatched actions.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useReducer(reducer, initialState)` returns `[state, dispatch]`. You describe *what happened* by dispatching actions, and a pure `reducer` function computes the next state.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: When many event handlers update related state in different ways, logic scatters. A reducer centralizes all transitions in one testable function.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content:
- Several pieces of state that change together.
- Next state depends on the previous state in complex ways.
- You want to unit test state logic without rendering.

codeExamples.title: Cart reducer
codeExamples.explanation: Components only dispatch descriptive actions. The reducer is a pure function you can test with plain inputs and outputs.

commonMistakes: Mutating state inside the reducer.
Running side effects (fetches, timers) inside the reducer — it must be pure.
realWorldExample: Multi-step forms, shopping carts and editors with undo often use reducers; `useReducer` + Context scales to app-level state.
interviewTip: Compare with useState: same capability, different organisation. Mention `dispatch` is stable between renders.

quiz.prompt: A reducer may call fetch() to load data.
quiz.explanation: Reducers must be pure; side effects go in event handlers or Effects.

flashcards.back: Yes, the dispatch function identity never changes.

title: useMemo
description: Cache the result of an expensive calculation between renders.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useMemo(calculate, deps)` caches the result of `calculate` and only recomputes it when a dependency changes.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content:
- Skip expensive recalculations (filtering 10,000 rows, heavy math).
- Keep an object or array **referentially stable** so a `memo`-wrapped child or an Effect dependency doesn't change every render.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content: Only after you notice a real performance issue, e.g. measured with the React Profiler. Most calculations are fast enough. With the **React Compiler** enabled, much of this memoization happens automatically.

codeExamples.title: Memoizing a filtered list
codeExamples.explanation: The filter only re-runs when `products` or `query` change — not when unrelated state (like a hover highlight) re-renders the table.

whenNotToUse: Cheap calculations like string concatenation or small array maps.
As a semantic guarantee — it's a performance hint only.
commonMistakes: Wrapping every value in useMemo "just in case" — it adds cost and noise.
Missing dependencies, leading to stale results.
Relying on useMemo for correctness; React may discard the cache.
realWorldExample: Data grids and charts memoize derived datasets so typing elsewhere on the page stays responsive.
interviewTip: Say when NOT to use it, and mention the React Compiler reduces manual memoization.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary purpose of useMemo?
quiz.explanation: useMemo caches a calculation's result between renders.

quiz.prompt: React guarantees it will never recompute a useMemo value while dependencies are unchanged.
quiz.explanation: It's a performance hint; React may drop cached values.

flashcards.back: A computed value.
The React DevTools Profiler.

interviewQuestion.question: When should you avoid useMemo?
interviewQuestion.answer: When the calculation is cheap, when dependencies change on almost every render anyway, or when the React Compiler already memoizes the component. Memoization has its own cost: storing values and comparing dependencies.

title: useCallback
description: Cache a function definition between renders.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useCallback(fn, deps)` returns the same function instance until a dependency changes. It's equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Every render creates new function objects. That's normally fine, but it breaks `React.memo` on children (props look different) and can re-trigger Effects that depend on the function.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content:
- Passing a callback to a `memo`-wrapped child that is expensive to render.
- A function used as an Effect dependency or returned from a custom Hook.

Otherwise skip it — and with the React Compiler it's rarely needed.

codeExamples.title: Stable callback for a memoized child
codeExamples.explanation: Because `handleSelect` keeps its identity, `List` skips re-rendering when `Page` re-renders for unrelated reasons.

commonMistakes: Using useCallback without a memoized consumer — it changes nothing.
Forgetting dependencies, so the callback reads stale state.
realWorldExample: Large virtualized lists pass stable row callbacks to keep scrolling smooth.
interviewTip: Explain that useCallback only helps when something compares the function identity.

quiz.prompt: useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to…
quiz.explanation: It memoizes the function itself.

flashcards.back: When a memoized child or an Effect depends on the function's identity.

title: useEffectEvent
description: Read the latest props and state inside an Effect without making them dependencies (React 19.2).

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useEffectEvent` (stable since React 19.2) creates an "Effect Event": a function you call from inside an Effect that always sees the latest props and state, but is **not** a dependency of that Effect.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Sometimes an Effect should re-synchronize when some values change (e.g. `roomId`) but merely *read* others (e.g. `theme` for a notification). Without Effect Events you either re-connect on every theme change or disable the lint rule.

sections.title: Rules
sections.content:
- Only call Effect Events from inside Effects.
- Don't pass them to other components or Hooks.
- Don't use them to hide dependencies that should re-run the Effect.

codeExamples.title: Reading theme without reconnecting
codeExamples.explanation: The Effect only reconnects when `roomId` changes. `onConnected` still reads the current `theme` when it fires.

commonMistakes: Using Effect Events to silence the dependency linter for values that *should* re-sync the Effect.
Calling an Effect Event during rendering.
realWorldExample: Analytics logging inside a subscription often needs the latest user settings without resubscribing.
interviewTip: Mention it's the official replacement for the old 'latest ref' pattern.

quiz.prompt: Effect Events should be listed in the Effect's dependency array.
quiz.explanation: They're intentionally non-reactive and are not dependencies.

flashcards.front: Which React version made useEffectEvent stable?
flashcards.back: React 19.2.

title: Render and Commit
description: How React turns components into pixels: trigger, render, commit.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content:
Every screen update goes through three steps:

- **Trigger:** initial render or a state update.
- **Render:** React calls your components to figure out what the UI should be.
- **Commit:** React applies the minimal changes to the DOM. Then the browser paints.

sections.title: Why does it matter?
sections.content: "Rendering" in React means calling your components, not touching the DOM. A component can render without any DOM change if its output is the same. Understanding this explains why pure rendering, memoization and Effects (which run after commit) work the way they do.

sections.title: Concurrent rendering
sections.content: Since React 18, the render phase can be interrupted for urgent updates (like typing) when you use features such as `useTransition`. The commit phase is always synchronous.

codeExamples.title: Logging the phases
codeExamples.explanation: "render" logs while React calculates the UI. The Effect logs after React has committed the changes to the DOM.

commonMistakes: Believing 'render' means 'update the DOM'.
Doing side effects during render, which may run multiple times.
realWorldExample: A clock re-renders every second, but React only updates the single text node that changed.
interviewTip: Describe trigger → render → commit in one breath; interviewers use it to test mental models.

quiz.prompt: Put React's update steps in order:
quiz.explanation: React renders first, then commits, then the browser paints.

flashcards.front: Which phase can be interrupted in concurrent React?
flashcards.back: The render phase. Commit is synchronous.

title: What Causes Re-renders
description: Know exactly when and why a component renders again.
keyConcepts: Props don't cause re-renders by themselves

sections.title: What causes a re-render?
sections.content:
1. Its own **state** changes.
2. Its **parent re-renders** (by default, all children re-render too).
3. A **context** it reads changes.

Props changing is really cause #2: props only change when the parent re-renders.

sections.title: Common misconception
sections.content: "A component re-renders when its props change" is incomplete. A child re-renders whenever its parent does, even with identical props — unless it's wrapped in `memo` (or optimized by the React Compiler).

sections.title: Is re-rendering bad?
sections.content: Usually no. Re-rendering is fast; React only commits real DOM changes. Optimize only when profiling shows slow renders.

codeExamples.title: Moving state down
codeExamples.explanation: Moving state into `SearchInput` means typing only re-renders the input, not `SlowChart`. Structure often fixes performance before memoization is needed.

commonMistakes: Assuming children only re-render when their props change.
Optimizing re-renders that aren't actually slow.
realWorldExample: Forms that live next to heavy charts often split into smaller components so typing stays instant.
interviewTip: List the three causes, then mention 'move state down' and 'lift content up (children)' as non-memo fixes.

quiz.prompt: A child component only re-renders when its props change.
quiz.explanation: By default children re-render whenever the parent does.

quiz.prompt: Which does NOT directly cause a re-render?
options: Calling the component's state setter with a new value
quiz.explanation: Refs are mutable boxes that never trigger renders.

flashcards.back: Own state change, parent re-render, consumed context change.

interviewQuestion.question: What causes a React component to re-render?
interviewQuestion.answer: A change to its own state, a re-render of its parent, or a change in a context it consumes. Props changing is a consequence of the parent re-rendering. `memo` and the React Compiler can skip re-renders when props are unchanged.

title: Reconciliation & the Virtual DOM
description: How React compares element trees to compute the minimal set of DOM updates.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Reconciliation is the algorithm React uses to compare the previous element tree with the new one and decide what to change in the DOM. People often call the element tree the "virtual DOM".

sections.title: The heuristics
sections.content:
A perfect tree diff is O(n³). React uses two assumptions to make it O(n):

- Elements of **different types** produce different trees — React tears down the old subtree and mounts a new one (state is lost).
- **Keys** identify which children are stable across renders.

sections.title: Position matters
sections.content: State is tied to a component's **position in the tree**. Rendering the same component type at the same position preserves state; changing the type or key at that position resets it.

sections.title: Fiber
sections.content: React's internal architecture (Fiber, since React 16) splits rendering into units of work so it can be paused, prioritized and resumed — the foundation of concurrent features.

codeExamples.title: Type change resets state
codeExamples.explanation: Toggling `isPaused` switches the parent element type between `div` and `section`, so React remounts the whole subtree and `Counter`'s state resets. Keep the same structure to preserve state.

commonMistakes: Saying the virtual DOM is always faster than direct DOM manipulation — its benefit is a declarative model with good-enough performance.
Not realizing that changing an element's type wipes its subtree's state.
realWorldExample: Swapping a `<table>` for a `<div>` layout when switching views resets all row state — a common real bug.
interviewTip: Mention the two heuristics (type and key) and that React 16+ uses the Fiber architecture.

quiz.prompt: When an element at the same position changes from <div> to <span>, React…
options: Destroys the old subtree and mounts a new one
quiz.explanation: Different types mean different trees; state below is reset.

flashcards.back: React's reconciliation engine that splits work into interruptible units.

interviewQuestion.question: What is reconciliation?
interviewQuestion.answer: It's the process of diffing the new React element tree against the previous one to find the minimum DOM changes. React assumes different element types produce different trees and uses keys to match children, which makes diffing linear time.

title: Strict Mode
description: A development-only tool that surfaces bugs by double-invoking renders and Effects.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `<StrictMode>` wraps part of your app and enables extra development checks. It renders nothing visible and has no effect in production builds.

sections.title: What it does
sections.content:
- Calls component functions (and initializers) **twice** to find impure rendering.
- Runs Effects **setup → cleanup → setup** on mount to find missing cleanup.
- Runs ref callbacks twice on mount (React 19) to check ref cleanup.
- Warns about deprecated APIs.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Concurrent rendering and features like Activity/Offscreen may mount and unmount components more than once. Strict Mode makes sure your code is resilient to that.

codeExamples.title: Enabling Strict Mode
codeExamples.explanation: Next.js enables Strict Mode by default in the App Router. Vite templates wrap `<App />` in `<StrictMode>`.

commonMistakes: Removing Strict Mode to hide the 'effect runs twice' behaviour instead of fixing cleanup.
Thinking Strict Mode affects production.
realWorldExample: Teams discover missing WebSocket cleanup because Strict Mode creates two connections in development.
interviewTip: Answer the classic 'why does my effect run twice?' with Strict Mode and cleanup.

quiz.prompt: Strict Mode double-invokes Effects in production builds.
quiz.explanation: All Strict Mode checks are development-only.

flashcards.back: No, it only enables dev checks.

title: Error Boundaries
description: Catch rendering errors in a subtree and show a fallback instead of a blank screen.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: An error boundary is a component that catches JavaScript errors thrown while rendering its children, logs them, and displays a fallback UI.

sections.title: How to create one
sections.content: Error boundaries are still **class components** implementing `static getDerivedStateFromError()` (to show a fallback) and/or `componentDidCatch()` (to log). Most apps use the small `react-error-boundary` package. In Next.js, `error.js` files create boundaries per route segment.

sections.title: What they don't catch
sections.content:
- Errors in event handlers (use try/catch).
- Async code like `setTimeout` callbacks.
- Errors in the boundary itself.
- Server-side rendering errors (frameworks handle those).

React 19 adds root options `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError` for reporting.

codeExamples.title: A minimal boundary
codeExamples.explanation: If `Comments` throws during render, the boundary swaps in the fallback while the rest of the page keeps working.

commonMistakes: Expecting boundaries to catch errors in event handlers.
Wrapping only the whole app, so one widget failure blanks the entire page.
realWorldExample: Dashboards wrap each widget in its own boundary so one broken chart doesn't take down the page.
interviewTip: Mention that function components can't be boundaries yet, and name react-error-boundary and Next.js error.js.

quiz.prompt: Which error does an error boundary catch?
options: A syntax error at build time
An error thrown while rendering a child
An error thrown in an onClick handler
quiz.explanation: Boundaries catch errors during rendering, lifecycle methods and constructors of their children.

flashcards.front: Can a function component be an error boundary?
flashcards.back: Not natively; use a class or react-error-boundary.

title: Performance Fundamentals
description: Measure first, then fix the real bottleneck.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: React performance work is about two things: **render cost** (how much work React does when state changes) and **load cost** (how much JavaScript the user downloads and executes).

sections.title: The process
sections.content:
1. Reproduce the slowness and measure (React DevTools Profiler, browser Performance panel, Web Vitals like INP and LCP).
2. Find the expensive component or interaction.
3. Apply the simplest fix: move state down, pass children, split code, virtualize long lists.
4. Memoize (`memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`) or enable the React Compiler.
5. Measure again.

sections.title: Load performance
sections.content: Ship less JavaScript: Server Components, code splitting with `lazy`, tree-shaking, smaller dependencies, optimized images.

codeExamples.title: Memoizing an expensive child
codeExamples.explanation: `memo` lets React skip re-rendering the chart while the user types, because `data` hasn't changed.

commonMistakes: Optimizing without measuring.
Wrapping everything in memo, adding complexity with no benefit.
realWorldExample: Teams track Interaction to Next Paint (INP) and fix slow handlers that block typing.
interviewTip: Always start with 'I'd measure first with the Profiler' — it signals seniority.

quiz.prompt: Order a sensible optimization workflow:
quiz.explanation: Measure → identify → fix → verify.

flashcards.back: Render cost and load (bundle) cost.

title: React.memo
description: Skip re-rendering a component when its props haven't changed.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `memo(Component)` returns a memoized version that re-renders only if its props changed, compared shallowly with `Object.is`.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: By default children re-render with their parent. For expensive components, skipping identical renders saves real time.

sections.title: Making it effective
sections.content: Props must be stable. A new object, array or function on every parent render defeats `memo`. Combine it with `useMemo`/`useCallback`, or let the React Compiler handle it.

codeExamples.title: memo defeated by an inline object
codeExamples.explanation: Shallow comparison treats `{ width: 40 }` as a new value each render. Passing primitives (or memoized objects) keeps props equal.

commonMistakes: Expecting memo to stop re-renders caused by the component's own state or context.
Passing inline objects/functions to memoized components.
realWorldExample: Rows in a large table are memoized so editing one row doesn't re-render thousands of others.
interviewTip: Explain shallow comparison and why stable references matter.

quiz.prompt: A memo-wrapped component never re-renders when its parent re-renders.
quiz.explanation: It still re-renders if props change by reference, or if its own state or a consumed context changes.

flashcards.back: Shallowly, using Object.is for each prop.

title: Lazy Loading with lazy()
description: Load a component's code only when it's first rendered.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `lazy(() => import('./Editor'))` declares a component whose code is downloaded the first time it renders. While loading, the nearest `<Suspense>` shows its fallback.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Users shouldn't download code for screens or heavy widgets they never open — admin panels, rich text editors, charts, modals.

sections.title: Rules
sections.content:
- The imported module must have a **default export** (or map a named export).
- Declare `lazy` components at module top level, not inside other components.
- Wrap them in `<Suspense>` with a fallback.

codeExamples.title: Lazy-loading a heavy editor
codeExamples.explanation: The editor's JavaScript is fetched only when the user clicks Edit. Suspense shows a fallback during the download.

commonMistakes: Declaring `lazy()` inside a component, which re-creates it and resets state.
Lazy-loading tiny components, adding network round-trips for little gain.
realWorldExample: Admin dashboards lazy-load chart libraries; editors lazy-load syntax highlighters.
interviewTip: Connect lazy to code splitting and Suspense; mention `next/dynamic` in Next.js.

quiz.prompt: What must wrap a lazy component while it loads?
quiz.explanation: Suspense displays the fallback until the code arrives.

flashcards.front: lazy() expects the module to have…
flashcards.back: A default export that is a component.

title: Code Splitting
description: Split your JavaScript bundle into chunks that load on demand.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Code splitting divides your app into multiple bundles. Bundlers (Vite, webpack, Turbopack) create a separate chunk wherever you use dynamic `import()`.

sections.title: Strategies
sections.content:
- **Route-based:** each page loads its own code. Frameworks like Next.js do this automatically.
- **Component-based:** heavy, rarely used UI (`lazy`, `next/dynamic`).
- **Library-based:** import big libraries only where needed: `const { format } = await import('date-fns')`.

sections.title: Trade-off
sections.content: More chunks mean more requests. Split where it saves meaningful bytes on the critical path, and consider prefetching likely next steps.

codeExamples.title: Splitting a library
codeExamples.explanation: A dynamic import inside an event handler keeps a large library out of the initial bundle.

commonMistakes: Splitting everything into tiny chunks, causing request waterfalls.
Forgetting a loading state for split components.
realWorldExample: Next.js automatically splits per route, so visiting /blog never downloads /dashboard code.
interviewTip: Mention route-based splitting as the highest-impact default.

quiz.prompt: Next.js automatically code-splits by route.
quiz.explanation: Each route segment gets its own bundle.

flashcards.front: What syntax creates a split point?
flashcards.back: Dynamic `import()`.

title: React DevTools & Profiler
description: Inspect components, props, state and render performance in the browser.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: React DevTools is a browser extension (and standalone app) that adds **Components** and **Profiler** tabs to developer tools.

sections.title: What you can do
sections.content:
- Inspect the component tree, props, state, hooks and context.
- Edit props/state live to test UI.
- Record a **Profiler** session to see which components rendered, how long they took and why.
- Turn on "Highlight updates when components render".
- React 19.2 adds custom **Performance tracks** to the browser's Performance panel showing scheduler and component work.

sections.title: Workflow
sections.content: Record the slow interaction, look for wide or frequently repeated bars in the flame graph, check "why did this render", then fix and record again.

codeExamples.title: Profiling in production-like builds
codeExamples.code:
# Profile a production build for realistic numbers
npm run build
npm run start

# Development builds are slower and include extra checks,
# so absolute timings there are inflated.
codeExamples.explanation: Development mode includes Strict Mode double renders and debugging overhead. Use it to find *which* components render, and production-like builds for *how long* they take.

commonMistakes: Treating development-mode timings as real-world performance.
Optimizing components that the Profiler shows are fast.
realWorldExample: Engineers find that a context provider re-renders the whole tree on every keystroke using the Profiler.
interviewTip: Describe a concrete profiling story: record, find the culprit, fix, verify.

quiz.prompt: Which DevTools tab shows how long each component took to render?
quiz.explanation: The Profiler records commits and render durations.

flashcards.front: Dev or prod builds for accurate timings?
flashcards.back: Production-like builds.

title: Performance Optimization Toolkit
description: A practical toolkit: virtualization, transitions, memoization, compiler and server rendering.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: Once you've measured a problem, choose the technique that matches it.

sections.title: Techniques by symptom
sections.content:
- **Typing feels laggy because a big list re-renders:** `useDeferredValue` for the list, or `useTransition` for the update.
- **Thousands of rows:** virtualize (render only visible rows) with libraries like TanStack Virtual.
- **Expensive pure components re-rendering:** `memo` + stable props, or the React Compiler.
- **Too much JavaScript on load:** Server Components, code splitting, removing heavy dependencies.
- **Too many network requests:** fetch in parallel, cache, prefetch.
- **Effects firing too often:** debounce/throttle, fix dependencies.

sections.title: Avoid premature optimization
sections.content: Each technique adds complexity. Apply it where measurement shows a problem.

codeExamples.title: Deferring an expensive list
codeExamples.explanation: The input updates immediately with `query`. `SlowResults` renders with the deferred value in the background; React can interrupt that work when the user types again. `memo` is required so the urgent render skips `SlowResults`.

commonMistakes: Using debouncing when the real fix is deferring rendering.
Forgetting `memo` with useDeferredValue, so the slow component still renders on every keystroke.
realWorldExample: Search pages with thousands of results combine virtualization with useDeferredValue to keep typing instant.
interviewTip: For the classic 'typing in search re-renders an expensive list' question: measure, isolate state, defer the list, memoize, virtualize.

quiz.prompt: Best technique for rendering 50,000 rows in a scrollable table?
quiz.explanation: Virtualization keeps DOM size small regardless of data size.

flashcards.back: So the urgent render can skip the slow component and only the deferred render does the heavy work.

title: Suspense
description: Declaratively show a fallback while part of the tree is waiting for code or data.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `<Suspense fallback={...}>` displays the fallback while any child is "suspended" — waiting for lazy-loaded code or data from a Suspense-enabled source.

sections.title: What can suspend?
sections.content:
- Components created with `lazy()`.
- Reading a promise with `use(promise)`.
- Data from Suspense-enabled frameworks and libraries (Next.js Server Components, TanStack Query's suspense mode, Relay).

Data fetched inside a `useEffect` does **not** trigger Suspense.

sections.title: Designing boundaries
sections.content: Place boundaries around independent parts of the page so fast content shows first. Nested boundaries reveal UI progressively. Transitions (`startTransition`) keep already-visible content on screen instead of flashing a fallback.

codeExamples.title: Nested Suspense boundaries
codeExamples.explanation: The header appears as soon as its data is ready; posts keep their own skeleton until they load.

commonMistakes: Expecting Suspense to work with data fetched in useEffect.
One giant boundary at the root so the whole page shows a spinner.
realWorldExample: Next.js `loading.js` files are Suspense boundaries; streaming HTML fills them in as data resolves.
interviewTip: Explain which sources can suspend and how nested boundaries enable progressive loading.

quiz.prompt: Data fetched in useEffect automatically triggers the nearest Suspense fallback.
quiz.explanation: Only Suspense-enabled sources (lazy, use(promise), frameworks) suspend.

flashcards.front: What does Suspense show while waiting?
flashcards.back: Its `fallback` prop.

title: useTransition
description: Mark state updates as non-urgent so the UI stays responsive.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()` lets you mark updates as **transitions**: low-priority work React can interrupt for urgent updates like typing or clicking.

sections.title: Why does it exist?
sections.content: Some updates trigger heavy renders (switching tabs, filtering big lists). Marking them as transitions keeps the current UI interactive and avoids hiding visible content behind Suspense fallbacks.

sections.title: React 19: async transitions
sections.content: In React 19 you can pass an **async** function to `startTransition`. These are called **Actions**: `isPending` stays true until the async work finishes, which is perfect for submissions.

codeExamples.title: Tab switch as a transition
codeExamples.explanation: Clicking Posts starts a transition. While SlowPosts renders, the old tab stays visible and interactive, and `isPending` shows a small spinner.

commonMistakes: Wrapping controlled input updates in a transition — inputs must update synchronously.
Expecting transitions to make slow code faster; they make it interruptible.
realWorldExample: Tab bars, router navigations and filters in data-heavy apps use transitions; Next.js navigations are transitions.
interviewTip: Contrast with useDeferredValue: transition wraps the *update*; deferred value wraps the *value*.

quiz.prompt: What does isPending from useTransition indicate?
options: A transition is still in progress
quiz.explanation: It is true while the transition's rendering (or async work) is ongoing.

flashcards.front: Async function in startTransition is called…
flashcards.back: An Action (React 19).

title: useDeferredValue
description: Defer re-rendering a non-urgent part of the UI.

sections.title: What is it?
sections.content: `useDeferredValue(value)` returns a version of the value that may "lag behind". React first re-renders with the old deferred value, then re-renders in the background with the new one.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.content: When you don't control the state update (e.g. it's a prop) but want a slow part of the UI to update with lower priority — like search results while typing.
